analysis.one_liner: Requires the ATF to build a searchable electronic database of gun sale records for crime tracing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, floor vote, or any action after its introduction in the Senate, and expired at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the ATF's National Tracing Center to build an electronic, searchable database of all firearm transaction records submitted by licensed dealers, and required every licensed dealer to keep their own records in electronic form the center could search remotely. The purpose is faster tracing of guns recovered at crime scenes back to their source. It also explicitly said this would apply even though Congress had restricted how ATF may use its funds for centralized gun records.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal, state, and local law enforcement, who could trace crime guns in hours instead of weeks or months; people in communities affected by gun crime; and small dealers who would benefit from faster, more modern tracing instead of paper records handled by phone and mail.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Police and communities affected by gun crime

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the ATF's National Tracing Center to establish and maintain electronic, searchable databases of all records of firearm importation, production, shipment, receipt, sale, or other disposition that licensees must submit.

It requires each licensed dealer, within three years, to keep electronic records that the National Tracing Center can access remotely, so traces no longer depend on paper files, faxes, and phone calls.

The center could search the databases only to obtain information related to a federal, state, local, tribal, or foreign crime, or foreign intelligence information, and the databases could not be searched by an individual's personally identifiable information.

The bill states it takes effect notwithstanding any other provision of law, including temporary or permanent restrictions placed on ATF funds — meaning it would override the appropriations limits that have kept gun-trace records decentralized.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers, who would bear the cost of digitizing all their records and keeping databases that a federal agency can search remotely, and gun owners who object to consolidated federal access to sale records.
analysis.who_pays_short: Licensed gun dealers and industry groups

drawbacks.text: Every licensed firearms dealer would have to convert to electronic, remotely accessible recordkeeping within three years, a real compliance cost that falls hardest on small independent dealers rather than large manufacturers.

The bill lets the National Tracing Center, with a state's permission, remotely query state firearms registration and pawnbroker databases, which expands federal access to state records and was likely to draw objections from lawmakers who oppose any consolidated federal gun database.
Electronic, remotely searchable records held by dealers could be a target for data breaches, creating a new security risk for small businesses holding customer information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is faster gun tracing for police, which the record search limits in the bill are designed to keep narrow. The main costs are digitization and maintenance for dealers, plus the objection in principle from those who oppose centralizing gun sale records where a federal agency can search them. The bill tried to address the second concern by banning searches by individuals' personally identifiable information and limiting searches to crime-related purposes, but opponents could still reasonably object to the precedent of remote federal access to dealer records.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing happened — no hearing, no vote, no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Leahy introduced the bill on May 24, 2018, with Sen. Bill Nelson as its only cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced.
No further action appears in the bill's record: it never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a Senate floor vote, and it died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

The bill was written to override funding restrictions on the ATF that prevent centralized gun-trace records, a measure long sought by the firearms industry and allied lawmakers, which helps explain the sparse support it drew.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed gun dealers and the firearms industry are better off: they avoided new digitization costs and remote federal access to their records, and the existing paper-based, decentralized tracing system stayed in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and the firearms industry

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Crime Gun Tracing Modernization Act in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Chair Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, never took up the bill after it was referred — no hearing or markup in the seven-plus months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's only support came from two Democrats, it drew no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would require every licensed dealer to digitize all sales records and maintain a database the ATF could search remotely — a direct cost to dealers and a check on the paper-based system dealers currently keep. Its purpose, faster crime-gun tracing, runs against the industry's preference for a decentralized record system.

They would submit records into a federal searchable database and lose the practical protection of the funding limits that keep ATF gun-trace records decentralized. The industry's interest in avoiding consolidated trace records runs against the bill's goal of faster police tracing.
